title: Preface
summary:
- SEC Form 10-K annual report for The AES Corporation for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2022.
- Cover information includes: SEC file number (1-12291), Delaware incorporation, Arlington, VA headquarters, contact details, and NYSE listings (AES common stock, AESC corporate units).
- Compliance status and classifications: well-known seasoned issuer, large accelerated filer, compliant with filing and interactive data requirements, auditor attestation of internal control over financial reporting, not a shell company, no restatement-related recovery analysis noted.
- Equity details: market value of non-affiliate equity as of June 30, 2022 (~$14.03 billion) and shares outstanding as of February 27, 2023 (668,824,617).
- Documents incorporated by reference: portions of the 2023 Proxy Statement into Parts II and III.
- Comprehensive table of contents outlining:
  - Part I: Business overview, Risk Factors, Unresolved Staff Comments, Properties, Legal Proceedings, Mine Safety Disclosures.
  - Part II: Market for equity securities and share matters, Selected Financial Data, MD&A (including executive summary, consolidated results, SBU performance analysis, key trends, liquidity/capital resources, critical accounting policies), market risk disclosures, audited financial statements and extensive footnotes.
  - Part III: Corporate governance, directors and executive officers, executive compensation, security ownership, related party transactions, auditor fees and services.
  - Part IV: Exhibits and financial statement schedule, signatures.
- Financial statements and notes cover key areas such as accounting policies, fair value, derivatives and hedging, receivables, investments, goodwill and intangibles, regulatory assets/liabilities, debt, leases, benefit plans, segments/geography, revenue, impairments, income taxes, dispositions/acquisitions, EPS, risks and uncertainties, related parties, quarterly data, and subsequent events.
- Glossary providing definitions of frequently used terms and acronyms, including AES subsidiaries and affiliates, non-GAAP measures (Adjusted EPS, Adjusted PTC), industry and regulatory bodies, environmental and market regulations, and operational terms relevant to the power and energy sector.

heading: PART I
start_phrase: In this Annual Report the terms “AES,” “the Company,” “us,” or “we” refer to The AES Corporation and all of its subsidiaries and affiliates, collectively.
summary:
- Defines terminology used throughout the report (AES, the Company, The AES Corporation, Parent Company).
- Provides a forward-looking statements disclaimer under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995, noting inherent uncertainties, non-comprehensiveness of listed factors, and no obligation to update.
- Summarizes extensive risk factors that could materially affect results, including:
  - Macroeconomic conditions (global and China-specific), demand for electricity, inflation, interest and foreign exchange rates.
  - Market risks: volatility in electricity and fuel prices, fuel availability and logistics, hedging effectiveness, credit support needs.
  - Financing and liquidity: access to capital markets, refinancing needs, debt covenants (recourse and non-recourse), revolver compliance, ability to upstream cash from subsidiaries, credit rating changes.
  - Operational risks: plant availability, outages, equipment failures, O&M cost management, reliability, competition, ability to secure long-term contracts and manage counterparty credit.
  - External events: weather variability (including hydrology, wind, solar resource), storms, wildfires, natural disasters, pandemics, and global supply-chain disruptions.
  - Development and strategy execution: capital raising for projects, execution of development pipeline, success of renewables and energy storage initiatives, availability of government incentives, ESG strategy execution, technology advancements.
  - Customer and structural factors: changes in customer counts/usage, performance of JVs and equity-method investees not controlled, achieving reasonable rate treatment at utilities.
  - Legal and regulatory: changes in domestic/international energy policy, environmental laws (GHG, emissions, CCR), regulatory oversight, tax law changes and challenges, litigation and investigations.
  - Transactional and financial reporting: acquisition performance, insurance adequacy, pension asset performance and funding obligations, asset impairments/disposals, changes in accounting, corporate governance, and securities law, internal control effectiveness.
  - Human capital and cyber: ability to attract/retain talent, cybersecurity risks, and data privacy.
- References where additional details appear (Item 1A—Risk Factors; Item 3—Legal Proceedings).
- Notes that Item 1—Business will outline company strategy and businesses by strategic business unit with key financial drivers, followed by an Executive Summary.

text:
Incorporated in 1981, AES is a global energy company accelerating the future of energy. Together with our many stakeholders, we are
improving lives by delivering the greener, smarter energy solutions the world needs. Our diverse workforce is committed to continuous innovation
and operational excellence, while partnering with our customers on their strategic energy transitions and continuing to meet their energy needs
today.

title: Our Strategy
heading: Our Strategy
start_phrase: AES is an industry leader in developing and operating the solutions that will enable the transition to zero and low-carbon sources of energy and achievement of the Paris Agreement's goal of net-zero emissions by 2050.
summary:
- Introduces AES as a global energy company focused on accelerating the transition to greener, smarter energy through innovation, partnerships, and operational excellence.
- Outlines strategy to lead in zero- and low-carbon solutions aligned with Paris net-zero by 2050, capitalizing on decarbonization, electrification, and digitalization.
- Emphasizes partnering with large corporate customers; recognized by BNEF in 2022 as the #1 global clean energy developer for corporations.
- Highlights 2022 commercial progress: 5.2 GW of renewables contracted; backlog reached ~12.2 GW; development pipeline expanded from 55 GW to 64 GW; proactive supply-chain and supplier arrangements; substantial 2023–2025 capex directed to renewables.
- Describes customer co-creation, including first-of-its-kind 24/7 carbon-free energy for data centers and a U.S. green hydrogen project with Air Products (≈1.4 GW of wind/solar; >200 MT/day H2).
- Details sector solutions such as “Green Blend” for mining in South America that integrates renewables with thermal to reduce emissions.
- Addresses utility transitions and Just Transition efforts; AES Indiana targeting retirement of remaining coal by end of 2025 while adding renewables and natural gas.
- Notes innovation engine AES Next, which incubates new technologies and business models to sustain competitive advantage.
- Summarizes 2022 strategic highlights: 5,153 MW of renewables/storage signed (including 2,553 MW in the U.S.); 1,943 MW completed across multiple countries; backlog of 12,179 MW (5,453 MW under construction; 6,726 MW with PPAs); upcoming internal management changes expected to modify reporting segments.
- Provides generation overview: 32,326 MW owned/operated (including AES Indiana) with diversified fuels; key performance drivers (contract mix, reliability, capacity availability, fuel costs, seasonality, economic activity, fixed-cost control, competition, and U.S. renewable tax credits); sales structure (medium-/long-term contracts vs short-term markets) and use of fuel pass-throughs or hedging when needed.
text:
Our Strategy
AES is an industry leader in developing and operating the solutions that will enable the transition to zero and low-carbon sources of energy
and achievement of the Paris Agreement's goal of net-zero emissions by 2050.
Today we see an enormous business opportunity from the once-in-a-lifetime transformation of the electricity sector driven by
decarbonization, electrification, and digitalization. There is a substantial need for more renewable energy as well as an opportunity for innovation
to develop new products and solutions that help customers accomplish their individual decarbonization goals.
The focus of our strategy continues to be on partnering with large companies that are looking to transition to carbon-free sources of
electricity. As an indication of our success, in 2022 we were recognized by BNEF as the #1 global clean energy developer for corporations.
In 2022, we signed long-term contracts for 5.2 GW of renewable power, bringing our backlog of projects — those with signed contracts, but
which are not yet in operation — to 12.2 GW. Our backlog serves as the core component of future growth.
Central to our renewables growth strategy is a focus on customer collaboration and co-creation, which helps us develop unique solutions
tailored to a specific customer's needs. This approach not only contributes to customer satisfaction and repeat business, but it also allows AES
to work with key customers on a bilateral basis rather than just through participation in bid processes.
This approach has led to the co-creation of several first-of-its-kind industry innovations, including agreements to supply 24/7 carbon-free
energy for global data center companies. Our unique capabilities in developing tailored energy solutions, enabled us to partner with Air Products
to announce our plans to develop, build, own, and operate the largest green hydrogen production facility to date in the United States.
We are also working with some of the world's largest mining companies in their transition to renewable energy in South America, essentially
reducing the emissions of major supply chains. One way in which we are serving the6 | 2022 Annual Report
mining industry is through our Green Blend offering, in which we work to integrate renewable energy with thermal power during select hours of
the day, reducing overall thermal generation and lowering emissions.
With our utilities, we are working with a broad range of stakeholders to transition to lower carbon forms of energy while promoting a Just
Transition for the workers and communities who may be negatively impacted by the closure of fossil fuel facilities. At AES Indiana, for example,
we are working to retire its remaining coal generation by the end of 2025, while adding new renewables and natural gas to the grid.
Our renewable growth strategy includes taking steps to ensure and enable growth in future years. We massively expanded our pipeline of
development projects, which grew from 55 GW in January 2022 to 64 GW as of the end of 2022, both through acquisitions and increased
investment in development activities, such as securing land or advancing permitting and interconnection processes. For our projects in late-
stage development, we worked to secure supplier arrangements to avoid any potential delays in relation to industry shortages, aided by our
scale, supplier relationships, and advanced planning measures. A substantial portion of our expected capital expenditures through 2025 will be
related to the development of renewable projects.
We are also developing and incubating new technologies that add value today and will drive our business in the future. We understand that
the energy industry is changing rapidly, and aim to proactively seek solutions that will give us a continued competitive advantage. At the core of
our innovation strategy is AES Next, our business and technology incubator. AES Next works to identify new and innovative technologies and
business opportunities that provide or support leading-edge greener energy solutions.

title: 2022 Strategic Highlights
heading: 2022 Strategic Highlights
start_phrase: •We signed 5,153 MW of renewables and energy storage under long-term PPAs, including 2,553 MW of solar, wind and energy storage in the United States.
summary:
- Emphasis on decarbonization through solutions like Green Blend, integrating renewables with thermal generation to cut emissions, particularly for mining customers.
- Commitment to a Just Transition for communities and workers affected by fossil facility closures; example: AES Indiana plans to retire remaining coal by end of 2025 while adding renewables and natural gas.
- Expansion of the renewable development pipeline from 55 GW (Jan 2022) to 64 GW (end of 2022) via acquisitions and increased development activities (land, permitting, interconnection).
- Proactive supply-chain and supplier arrangements for late-stage projects to mitigate industry shortages; significant capital expenditures through 2025 dedicated to renewable project development.
- Innovation driven by AES Next, the company’s incubator for new technologies and business models that enable greener energy solutions.
- 2022 strategic results:
  - 5,153 MW of renewables and energy storage signed under long-term PPAs (including 2,553 MW in the U.S.).
  - 1,943 MW constructed or acquired and operational across the U.S., Brazil, the Dominican Republic, Chile, and Colombia (primarily wind, solar, and storage).
  - Backlog of 12,179 MW, comprising 5,453 MW under construction and 6,726 MW with signed PPAs not yet under construction.
  - Partnership with Air Products to develop the largest U.S. green hydrogen facility, supported by ~1.4 GW of wind/solar and electrolyzers producing over 200 metric tons per day.
  - Anticipated internal management changes leading to updates in financial reporting segments.
- Generation overview: 32,326 MW owned/operated portfolio (including AES Indiana), diversified by fuel type.
- Key performance drivers: contract structures, plant reliability/flexibility, capacity availability, fuel costs, seasonality, weather, economic activity, fixed-cost management, competition, and the ability to complete renewables construction and capture U.S. renewable tax credits.
- Sales and contracting approach: predominance of medium- and long-term contracts versus short-term market sales; fuel-based contracts generally include variable cost pass-throughs or tolling; when pass-throughs are absent, the company hedges or secures fuel supply agreements aligned with contract terms.
text:
2022 Strategic Highlights
•We signed 5,153 MW of renewables and energy storage under long-term PPAs, including 2,553 MW of solar, wind and energy storage in
the United States.
•We completed the construction or acquisition of operating projects totaling 1,943 MW in the United States, Brazil, the Dominican Republic,
Chile and Colombia, primarily wind, solar and energy storage.
•Our backlog, which includes projects with signed contracts, but which are not yet operational, is now 12,179 MW, consisting of:
◦5,453 MW under construction; and
◦6,726 MW with signed PPAs, but that are not yet under construction.
•We announced a partnership with Air Products to develop, build, own and operate the largest green hydrogen production facility to date in
the United States.
◦Includes approximately 1.4 GW of wind and solar generation, along with electrolyzer capacity capable of producing over 200 metric tons
per day (MT/D) of green hydrogen.
•The Company expects to announce certain internal management changes which will result in modifications to its financial reporting
segments.

summary:
Generation
We currently own and/or operate a generation portfolio of 32,326 MW, including generation from our integrated utility, AES Indiana. Our
generation fleet is diversified by fuel type. See discussion below under Fuel Costs.
Performance drivers of our generation businesses include types of electricity sales agreements, plant reliability and flexibility, availability of
generation capacity to meet contracted sales, fuel costs, seasonality, weather variations, economic activity, fixed-cost management, and
competition. The financial performance of our renewables business is also impacted by our ability to complete construction projects and earn
U.S. renewable tax credits.

- Highlights innovation through AES Next, the company’s incubator for emerging clean energy technologies and business models.
- 2022 strategic results:
  - 5,153 MW of renewables and storage signed under long-term PPAs (2,553 MW in the U.S.).
  - 1,943 MW placed in service or acquired across the U.S. and Latin America (primarily wind, solar, storage).
  - Backlog of 12,179 MW (5,453 MW under construction; 6,726 MW with signed PPAs).
  - Partnership with Air Products to build the largest U.S. green hydrogen facility, powered by ~1.4 GW of wind/solar and capable of >200 MT/day of green hydrogen.
  - Anticipated internal management changes affecting financial reporting segments.
- Provides a generation overview: 32,326 MW owned/operated (including AES Indiana), diversified by fuel; performance drivers include contract structure, reliability/flexibility, capacity availability, fuel costs, seasonality, economic activity, fixed-cost management, competition, and U.S. renewable tax credits.
- Explains contract sales (medium/long-term) structures that recover variable costs via pass-throughs or hedges, include capacity payments to cover fixed costs and return on capital, align currency of revenues/costs, and hedge interest rate exposure to mitigate price, fuel, FX, and rate risks.
- Details short-term sales in competitive markets, merit-order dispatch, higher sensitivity to market prices, provision of ancillary services, and participation in capacity markets that pay for availability.
- Discusses fuel cost management: long-term supply agreements or hedges for contracted plants, indexation alignment, tolling where offtakers supply fuel; short-term procurement for merchant plants; exposure to commodity price volatility.
- Notes that 46% of AES’s generation capacity is renewable (hydro, solar, wind, storage, biomass, landfill gas) with minimal fuel costs.
text:
Contract Sales — Most of our generation businesses sell electricity under medium- or long-term contracts ("contract sales") or under short-
term agreements in competitive markets ("short-term sales"). Our medium-term contract sales have terms of two to five years, while our long-
term contracts have terms of more than five years.
Contracts requiring fuel to generate energy, such as natural gas or coal, are structured to recover variable costs, including fuel and variable
O&M costs, either through direct or indexation-based contractual pass-throughs or tolling arrangements. When the contract does not include a
fuel pass-through, we typically hedge fuel costs or enter into fuel or energy supply agreements for a similar contract period (see discussion
below under Fuel Costs). These7 | 2022 Annual Report
contracts also help us to fund a significant portion of the total capital cost of the project through long-term non-recourse project-level financing.
Certain contracts include capacity payments that cover projected fixed costs of the plant, including fixed O&M expenses, debt service, and
a return on capital invested. In addition, most of our contracts require that the majority of the capacity payments be denominated in the currency
matching our fixed costs.
Contracts that do not have significant fuel cost or do not contain a capacity payment are structured based on long-term spot prices with
some negotiated pass-through costs, allowing us to recover expected fixed and variable costs as well as provide a return on investment.
These contracts are intended to reduce exposure to the volatility of fuel and electricity prices by linking the business's revenues and costs.
We generally structure our business to eliminate or reduce foreign exchange risk by matching the currency of revenue and expenses, including
fixed costs and debt. Our project debt may consist of both fixed and floating rate debt for which we typically hedge a significant portion of our
exposure. Some of our contracted businesses also receive a regulated market-based capacity payment, which is discussed in more detail in the
Short-Term Sales section below.
Thus, these contracts, or other related commercial arrangements, significantly mitigate our exposure to changes in power and, as
applicable, fuel prices, currency fluctuations and changes in interest rates. In addition, these contracts generally provide for a recovery of our
fixed operating expenses and a return on our investment, as long as we operate the plant to the reliability and efficiency standards required in
the contract.

title: Short-Term Sales
heading: Short-Term Sales —
start_phrase: Our other generation businesses sell power and ancillary services under short-term contracts with average terms of less than two years, including spot sales, directly in the short-term market or at regulated prices.
summary:
- Describes how long-term contracts underpin project-level, non-recourse financing and often include capacity payments designed to cover fixed O&M, debt service, and provide a return on capital.
- Explains contract structures that mitigate exposure to power and fuel price volatility, foreign exchange, and interest rate changes by using capacity payments, currency matching of revenues/expenses/debt, and hedging of floating-rate exposure.
- Notes alternative long-term arrangements without significant fuel costs or capacity payments that reference spot prices with pass-through costs to recover fixed and variable costs.
- Details short-term/spot sales in system-operator markets using merit order dispatch, making earnings more sensitive to market power prices.
- Highlights participation in ancillary service markets (e.g., voltage support, frequency regulation, spinning reserves) across the portfolio.
- Outlines regulated capacity markets that pay for availability, typically priced on cost of new entry and reserve margins, supplementing energy revenues.
- Emphasizes plant reliability and operational flexibility to meet contract standards, capture peak prices, and maximize market and ancillary revenues.
- Covers fuel cost management: long-term fuel supply agreements and financial hedges for contracted plants; indexation alignment; tolling where the offtaker supplies fuel; short-term fuel procurement for market-based sales; acknowledges commodity price risk.
- States that 46% of generation capacity is from renewables (hydro, solar, wind, storage, biomass, landfill gas) with minimal fuel costs.
text:
Short-Term Sales — Our other generation businesses sell power and ancillary services under short-term contracts with average terms of
less than two years, including spot sales, directly in the short-term market or at regulated prices. The short-term markets are typically
administered by a system operator to coordinate dispatch. Short-term markets generally operate on merit order dispatch, where the least
expensive generation facilities, based upon variable cost or bid price, are dispatched first and the most expensive facilities are dispatched last.
The short-term price is typically set at the marginal cost of energy or bid price (the cost of the last plant required to meet system demand). As a
result, the cash flows and earnings associated with these businesses are more sensitive to fluctuations in the market price for electricity. In
addition, many of these wholesale markets include markets for ancillary services to support the reliable operation of the transmission system.
Across our portfolio, we provide a wide array of ancillary services, including voltage support, frequency regulation and spinning reserves.
Many of the short-term markets in which we operate include regulated capacity markets. These capacity markets are intended to provide
additional revenue based upon availability without reliance on the energy margin from the merit order dispatch. Capacity markets are typically
priced based on the cost of a new entrant and the system capacity relative to the desired level of reserve margin (generation available in excess
of peak demand). Our generating facilities selling in the short-term markets typically receive capacity payments based on their availability in the
market.

title: Plant Reliability and Flexibility
heading: Plant Reliability and Flexibility —
start_phrase: Our contract and short-term sales provide incentives to our generation plants to optimally manage availability, operating efficiency and flexibility.
summary:
- The company structures long-term contracts to support non-recourse project financing, with capacity payments designed to cover fixed O&M, debt service, and a return on invested capital, typically denominated in the same currency as costs.
- Contracts and related hedges mitigate exposure to power and fuel price volatility, foreign exchange fluctuations, and interest rate changes; project debt may be a mix of fixed and floating rates with significant hedging.
- Some contracted assets also earn regulated, market-based capacity payments; overall, contracts aim to recover fixed expenses and ensure returns if reliability and efficiency standards are met.
- Short-term sales (average terms under two years) are made into merit-order wholesale markets where prices are set by the marginal unit, making cash flows more sensitive to market price swings.
- The portfolio provides ancillary services (e.g., voltage support, frequency regulation, spinning reserves), and many markets include capacity payments based on plant availability, tied to cost of new entry and reserve margins.
- Operational focus emphasizes plant reliability and flexibility to meet contractual standards, capture peak prices, and maximize ancillary revenues.
- Fuel cost management for thermal plants includes long-term fuel supply agreements, financial hedging, indexation alignment, and tolling arrangements where offtakers supply fuel; short-term sales rely on short-term fuel procurement and are exposed to fuel price volatility.
- 46% of generation capacity is from renewables (hydro, solar, wind, energy storage, biomass, landfill gas) with minimal fuel costs.
text:
Plant Reliability and Flexibility — Our contract and short-term sales provide incentives to our generation plants to optimally manage
availability, operating efficiency and flexibility. Capacity payments under contract sales are frequently tied to meeting minimum standards. In
short-term sales, our plants must be reliable and flexible to capture peak market prices and to maximize market-based revenues. In addition, our
flexibility allows us to capture ancillary service revenue while meeting local market needs.

title: Fuel Costs
heading: Fuel Costs —
start_phrase: For our thermal generation plants, fuel is a significant component of our total cost of generation.
summary:
- Overview of contracted sales for generation assets, including capacity payments that cover fixed costs, debt service, and return on capital, often denominated to match cost currencies and frequently hedged for interest rate and FX exposure.
- Explanation of contracts without fuel costs or without capacity payments, structured around long-term spot prices with pass-throughs to align revenues with costs and limit commodity price volatility.
- Description of how commercial arrangements mitigate exposure to power and fuel price changes, currency fluctuations, and interest rate shifts, contingent on meeting reliability and efficiency standards.
- Short-term sales model: merchant sales and ancillary services in system-operator markets using merit-order dispatch; greater earnings sensitivity to market prices; participation in ancillary services and capacity markets with availability-based payments.
- Emphasis on plant reliability, efficiency, and operational flexibility to meet contract standards and capture peak pricing and ancillary revenues.
- Fuel cost management strategies: long-term fuel supply agreements, financial hedging, index-linked arrangements, tolling structures, and short-term procurement for merchant plants; reference to commodity price risk.
- Generation portfolio fuel mix: 46% renewables (hydro, solar, wind, storage, biomass, landfill gas), 32% natural gas (including LNG imports in the Dominican Republic and Panama, otherwise local supply), 20% coal (domestic and international sourcing), and 2% pet coke/diesel/oil.
- Note on global sourcing programs to enhance purchasing power for fuels.
- Impacts of seasonality, weather patterns, renewable resource variability, hydrology, and local economic activity on output, margins, and prices.
- Focus on fixed-cost management across all generation businesses, with recovery of most fixed O&M via contracted capacity payments.
- Competitive dynamics: limited competition under medium- and long-term contracts; market-driven dispatch and prices for short-term sales.
- Utilities segment overview: AES Indiana (integrated utility) and AES Ohio (T&D) in the U.S., plus four distribution utilities in El Salvador; total of 2.6 million customers and 3,495 MW of U.S. utility generation capacity; limited competition in El Salvador with option for large customers to become unregulated.
- Utility business model and performance drivers: regulated rate of return, tariff structures, seasonality, weather, economic activity, and service reliability; utility revenues classified as regulated.
- Regulatory framework for rates: allowed return based on regulatory asset base, capital structure, and cost of capital; “used and useful” asset base; recovery of allowed returns and reasonable expenses through tariffs, which are periodically reviewed and may include pass-throughs for fuel and purchased power.
text:
Fuel Costs — For our thermal generation plants, fuel is a significant component of our total cost of generation. For contract sales, we often
enter into fuel supply agreements to match the contract period, or we may financially hedge our fuel costs. Some of our contracts include
indexation for fuels. In those cases, we seek to match our fuel supply agreements to the indexation. For certain projects, we have tolling
arrangements where the power offtaker is responsible for the supply and cost of fuel to our plants.
In short-term sales, we sell power at market prices that are generally reflective of the market cost of fuel at the time, and thus procure fuel
supply on a short-term basis, generally designed to match up with our market sales profile. Since fuel price is often the primary determinant for
power prices, the economics of projects with short-term sales are often subject to volatility of relative fuel prices. For further information
regarding commodity price risk please see Item 7A.—Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures about Market Risk in this Form 10-K.
46% of the capacity of our generation plants are fueled by renewables, including hydro, solar, wind, energy storage, biomass and landfill
gas, which do not have significant fuel costs.8 | 2022 Annual Report
32% of the capacity of our generation plants are fueled by natural gas. With the exception of our plants in the Dominican Republic and
Panama, where we import LNG to utilize in the local market, we use gas from local suppliers in each market.
20% of the capacity of our generation fleet is coal-fired. In the U.S., most of our coal-fired plants are supplied from domestic coal. At our
non-U.S. generation plants, and at our plant in Puerto Rico, we source coal from a mix of sources from the international market and in the local
jurisdictions. To the extent possible, we utilize our global sourcing program to maximize the purchasing power of our fuel procurement.
2% of the capacity of our generation fleet utilizes pet coke, diesel or oil for fuel. We source oil and diesel locally at prices linked to
international markets. We largely source pet coke from Mexico and the U.S.

title: Seasonality, Weather Variations and Economic Activity
heading: Seasonality, Weather Variations and Economic Activity —
start_phrase: Our generation businesses are affected by seasonal weather patterns and, therefore, operating margin is not generated evenly throughout the year.
summary:
- Fuel mix and sourcing for generation: 32% natural gas (mostly locally sourced; LNG imported for Dominican Republic and Panama), 20% coal (U.S. plants use domestic coal; non-U.S. and Puerto Rico source internationally and locally), 2% pet coke/diesel/oil (oil/diesel sourced locally at international-linked prices; pet coke largely from Mexico and the U.S.); use of a global sourcing program to enhance purchasing power.
- Operational drivers for generation: seasonality and weather variability (temperature, solar, wind, hydrology) affect output and margins; local economic activity influences demand and short-term power prices in competitive markets.
- Cost management: emphasis on managing and reducing fixed O&M costs; in long-term contracted plants, most fixed costs are recovered via capacity payments.
- Competitive dynamics: limited competition during medium- and long-term contract periods; short-term dispatch and prices set by market competition and local reliability rules.
- Utilities portfolio overview: AES operates six utilities—AES Indiana and AES Ohio in the U.S. plus four in El Salvador—serving 2.6 million customers; U.S. utilities include 3,495 MW of generation capacity.
- U.S. utility operations: AES Indiana is fully integrated (generation, transmission, distribution); AES Ohio handles transmission and distribution; both are sole distributors in their jurisdictions.
- El Salvador utilities: limited competition due to high entry barriers; large regulated customers may opt to become unregulated and procure directly from generators or marketers.
- Utility performance drivers: regulated rate of return and tariffs, seasonality, weather, economic activity, and service reliability; utility revenues classified as regulated.
- Regulation and tariffs: regulators set tariff frameworks and service standards; utilities earn an allowed return based on a defined regulatory asset base, capital structure, and cost of capital; allowed returns and reasonable operating expenses are recovered through tariffs.
- Tariff mechanics: subject to periodic review/reset; typically usage-based and may include pass-through of non-controllable costs (e.g., fuel for integrated utilities and purchased energy).
text:
Our generation businesses are affected by seasonal weather patterns and,
therefore, operating margin is not generated evenly throughout the year. Additionally, weather variations, including temperature, solar and wind
resources, and hydrological conditions, may also have an impact on generation output at our renewable generation facilities. In competitive
markets for power, local economic activity can also have an impact on power demand and short-term prices for power.

title: Fixed-Cost Management
heading: Fixed-Cost Management —
start_phrase: In our businesses with long-term contracts, the majority of the fixed O&M costs are recovered through the capacity payment.
summary:
- Fuel mix and sourcing: 32% of generation capacity fueled by natural gas (mostly locally sourced; LNG imports in Dominican Republic and Panama); 20% coal (domestic in U.S., mix of international/local elsewhere, including Puerto Rico); 2% pet coke, diesel or oil (oil/diesel sourced locally at international-linked prices; pet coke largely from Mexico and the U.S.); use of a global sourcing program to optimize fuel procurement.
- Operational drivers: seasonality and weather variability affect margins and renewable output (temperature, solar/wind resources, hydrology); local economic activity influences demand and power prices in competitive markets.
- Cost management: in long-term contracted generation, fixed O&M largely recovered via capacity payments; ongoing fixed-cost reduction is a key performance driver across generation.
- Competition: limited during medium/long-term contract terms; short-term sales subject to market competition and dispatch/reliability rules.
- Utility portfolio: AES operates six utilities—AES Indiana and AES Ohio in the U.S. plus four in El Salvador—serving 2.6 million customers; U.S. utilities include 3,495 MW of generation.
- U.S. utility roles: AES Indiana is fully integrated (generation, transmission, distribution); AES Ohio is a transmission and distribution regulated utility; both are sole distributors in their territories.
- El Salvador utilities: limited competition due to entry barriers; large regulated customers may opt out to buy directly from generators/commercializers.
- Utility revenue model and regulation: revenues classified as regulated; tariffs and service standards set by regulators; utilities earn an allowed rate of return based on regulatory asset base, capital structure, and cost of capital; reasonable O&M and allowed returns recovered through tariffs, which are periodically reviewed and may include pass-throughs for fuel or purchased energy costs.
text:
Fixed-Cost Management — In our businesses with long-term contracts, the majority of the fixed O&M costs are recovered through the
capacity payment. However, for all generation businesses, managing fixed costs and reducing them over time is a driver of business
performance.

title: Competition
heading: Competition —
start_phrase: For our businesses with medium- or long-term contracts, there is limited competition during the term of the contract.
summary:
- Fuel mix and sourcing: 32% of generation capacity is natural-gas fired (primarily locally sourced; LNG imported for Dominican Republic and Panama), 20% coal (U.S. plants use domestic coal; non-U.S. and Puerto Rico source internationally; global sourcing used to optimize procurement), and 2% pet coke/diesel/oil (oil and diesel sourced locally at international-linked prices; pet coke mainly from Mexico and the U.S.).
- Operating drivers: Seasonality and weather (temperature, wind/solar resources, hydrology) affect output and margins, especially for renewables; local economic activity influences demand and short-term power prices in competitive markets.
- Cost management: In long-term contracted generation, capacity payments recover most fixed O&M; across all generation businesses, reducing fixed costs remains a key performance lever.
- Competition: Limited during medium- and long-term contract periods; short-term sales subject to market competition and dispatch/reliability rules.
- Utilities overview: Six utilities (AES Indiana, AES Ohio, and four in El Salvador) serve 2.6 million customers; U.S. utilities include 3,495 MW of generation. AES Indiana is fully integrated (generation, transmission, distribution); AES Ohio is transmission and distribution only. El Salvador distribution faces limited competition; large regulated customers may opt to become unregulated and buy directly from generators/marketers.
- Utility revenue and performance: Utility revenues are regulated. Key drivers include allowed rate of return and tariff design, seasonality, weather, economic activity, and service reliability.
- Regulation and tariffs: Regulators set tariffs and service standards. Utilities earn a regulated return on an allowed regulatory asset base (assets deemed used and useful), considering capital structure and cost of capital. Tariffs recover the allowed return and reasonable operating expenses, are periodically reviewed/reset, are typically usage-based, and often include pass-through mechanisms for uncontrollable costs such as fuel and purchased power.
text:
Competition — For our businesses with medium- or long-term contracts, there is limited competition during the term of the contract. For
short-term sales, plant dispatch and the price of electricity are determined by market competition and local dispatch and reliability rules.

title: Utilities - Introduction
heading: Utilities
start_phrase: Our utility businesses consist of AES Indiana and AES Ohio in the U.S. and four utilities in El Salvador.
summary: AES’s Utilities segment includes AES Indiana, AES Ohio, and four distribution utilities in El Salvador, serving 2.6 million customers; the two U.S. utilities also have 3,495 MW of generation capacity. AES Indiana is a fully integrated utility (generation, transmission, distribution), and AES Ohio operates transmission and distribution; both are sole distributors in their jurisdictions. In El Salvador, distribution faces limited competition due to market entry barriers, though regulation allows large regulated customers to become unregulated users and contract directly with generators or commercialization agents. Utilities sell and bill end-users directly, with key performance drivers including regulated rate of return, tariffs, seasonality, weather, economic activity, and service reliability; utility revenue is classified as regulated on the Consolidated Statements of Operations.
text:
Utilities
Our utility businesses consist of AES Indiana and AES Ohio in the U.S. and four utilities in El Salvador. AES' six utility businesses distribute
power to 2.6 million customers and AES' two utilities in the U.S. also include generation capacity totaling 3,495 MW.
AES Indiana, our fully integrated utility, and AES Ohio, our transmission and distribution regulated utility, operate as the sole distributors of
electricity within their respective jurisdictions. AES Indiana owns and operates all of the facilities necessary to generate, transmit and distribute
electricity. AES Ohio owns and operates all of the facilities necessary to transmit and distribute electricity. At our distribution business in El
Salvador, we face limited competition due to significant barriers to enter the market. According to El Salvador's regulation, large regulated
customers have the option of becoming unregulated users and requesting service directly from generation or commercialization agents.
In general, our utilities sell electricity directly to end-users, such as homes and businesses, and bill customers directly. Key performance
drivers for utilities include the regulated rate of return and tariff, seasonality, weather variations, economic activity and reliability of service.
Revenue from utilities is classified as regulated on the Consolidated Statements of Operations.

title: Regulated Rate of Return and Tariff
heading: Regulated Rate of Return and Tariff —
start_phrase: In exchange for the right to sell or distribute electricity in a service territory, our utility businesses are subject to government regulation.
summary:
- Generation fuel mix and sourcing: 32% natural gas (mostly local gas; LNG imports in Dominican Republic and Panama), 20% coal (U.S. plants use domestic coal; non-U.S. and Puerto Rico source internationally and locally with global procurement), 2% pet coke/diesel/oil (oil/diesel priced to international markets; pet coke mainly from Mexico and the U.S.).
- Operating drivers for generation: seasonality and weather impact output and margins, especially for renewables; local economic activity influences demand and short-term prices; fixed-cost management is critical, with fixed O&M largely recovered via capacity payments in long-term contracts; competition limited under medium/long-term contracts, market-based for short-term sales.
- Utilities footprint and model: AES operates AES Indiana (integrated) and AES Ohio (T&D) in the U.S. plus four distribution utilities in El Salvador, serving 2.6 million customers; U.S. utilities include 3,495 MW of generation. Limited competition in El Salvador; large customers can opt out to unregulated service.
- Utility revenue and performance: revenue is regulated; regulators set tariffs and service standards. Allowed return based on regulatory asset base, capital structure, and cost of capital; tariffs recover allowed return and reasonable O&M, with pass-through mechanisms for fuel/purchased power. Some high-demand customers may be unregulated but pay non-bypassable distribution fees. Utilities must manage costs to tariff levels, address uncollectibles, and control losses.
- Utility operating factors: margins affected by seasonality and weather; sales influenced by customer count, temperature deviations, economic conditions, energy efficiency, and distributed generation; reliability standards apply, with potential incentives or penalties tied to outage duration and frequency.
- Development and construction: AES develops new generation and utility assets/retrofits to meet customer needs or regulatory requirements, prioritizing renewables in key growth markets. Investment decisions weigh strategic fit and risk-adjusted returns versus alternative uses of capital. The company often secures long-term offtake contracts pre-construction, seeks non-recourse project financing and partners, and uses third-party EPC with in-house construction oversight on budget, safety, and productivity.
- Segment structure and performance metric: operations organized into four SBUs—US and Utilities; South America (Chile, Colombia, Argentina, Brazil); MCAC (Mexico, Central America, Caribbean); and Eurasia (Europe, Asia). Two business lines: generation across all SBUs and utilities primarily in US and Utilities; utilities may also participate in wholesale markets. Performance measured by Adjusted PTC (non-GAAP), with SBU-level contributions referenced to the MD&A.
text:
Regulated Rate of Return and Tariff — In exchange for the right to sell or distribute electricity in a service territory, our utility businesses are
subject to government regulation. This regulation sets the framework for the prices ("tariffs") that our utilities are allowed to charge customers for
electricity and establishes service standards that we are required to meet.
Our utilities are generally permitted to earn a regulated rate of return on assets, determined by the regulator based on the utility's allowed
regulatory asset base, capital structure and cost of capital. The asset base on which the utility is permitted a return is determined by the
regulator, within the framework of applicable local laws, and is based on the amount of assets that are considered used and useful in serving
customers. Both the allowed return and the asset base are important components of the utility's earning power. The allowed rate of return and
operating expenses deemed reasonable by the regulator are recovered through the regulated tariff that the utility charges to its customers.
The tariff may be reviewed and reset by the regulator from time to time depending on local regulations, or the utility may seek a change in
its tariffs. The tariff is generally based upon usage level and may include a pass-through of costs that are not controlled by the utility, such as the
costs of fuel (in the case of integrated utilities) and/or the costs of purchased energy, to the customer. Components of the tariff that are directly
passed through to the9 | 2022 Annual Report
customer are usually adjusted through a summary regulatory process or an existing formula-based mechanism. In some regulatory regimes,
customers with demand above an established level are unregulated and can choose to contract directly with the utility or with other retail energy
suppliers and pay non-bypassable fees, which are fees to the distribution company for use of its distribution system.
The regulated tariff generally recognizes that our utility businesses should recover certain operating and fixed costs, as well as manage
uncollectible amounts, quality of service and technical and non-technical losses. Utilities, therefore, need to manage costs to the levels reflected
in the tariff, or risk non-recovery of costs or diminished returns.

title: Seasonality, Weather Variations, and Economic Activity
heading: Seasonality, Weather Variations, and Economic Activity —
start_phrase: Our utility businesses are generally affected by seasonal weather patterns and, therefore, operating margin is not generated evenly throughout the year.
summary:
- Regulatory framework and tariffs: Explanation of how utility customer rates are set via summary regulatory processes or formula mechanisms; treatment of large-demand customers who may be unregulated but pay non-bypassable distribution fees; emphasis that regulated tariffs are designed to recover operating and fixed costs, manage uncollectibles, service quality, and technical/non-technical losses; utilities must control costs to avoid under-recovery or reduced returns.
- Demand drivers and seasonality: Discussion of how seasonal weather patterns, temperature deviations, customer counts, historic usage, local economic activity, energy efficiency, and distributed generation affect retail sales and operating margins.
- Reliability standards: Utilities are required to meet explicit or implicit reliability metrics (outage duration/frequency) with potential incentives or penalties tied to performance.
- Development and construction strategy: Approach to building or retrofitting generation assets for utility needs or regulatory compliance; requirement for regulatory approvals to ensure capital recovery and returns; focus on developing renewable projects in key growth markets leveraging global scale; investment decisions based on strategic fit, risk-adjusted returns, and alternative capital uses; use of long-term offtake contracts, non-recourse project financing, and partnerships to limit parent equity; third-party construction with internal oversight on budget, safety, efficiency, and productivity.
- Segment organization: Company structured into four SBUs by geography—US and Utilities (United States, Puerto Rico, El Salvador), South America (Chile, Colombia, Argentina, Brazil), MCAC (Mexico, Central America, Caribbean), and Eurasia (Europe, Asia); two business lines—generation (all SBUs) and utilities (US and Utilities SBU) covering generation/purchase, distribution, transmission, and retail sales, with some wholesale activity.
- Performance measurement: Use of Adjusted PTC (a non-GAAP metric) to assess SBU operating performance, with 2022 contributions by SBU referenced and reconciliation/definitions provided in the MD&A.
text:
Our utility businesses are generally affected by seasonal weather patterns and,
therefore, operating margin is not generated evenly throughout the year. Additionally, weather variations may also have an impact based on the
number of customers, temperature variances from normal conditions, and customers' historic usage levels and patterns. Retail sales, after
adjustments for weather variations, are also affected by changes in local economic activity, energy efficiency and distributed generation
initiatives, as well as the number of retail customers.

title: Reliability of Service
heading: Reliability of Service —
start_phrase: Our utility businesses must meet certain reliability standards, such as duration and frequency of outages.
summary:
- Regulatory framework and tariffs: Utilities recover operating and fixed costs through regulated tariffs, which may include mechanisms for adjusting prices and recovering uncollectible amounts, service quality, and system losses. Some high-demand customers are unregulated, can contract directly with utilities or other suppliers, and pay non-bypassable distribution fees. Utilities must control costs to levels reflected in tariffs to avoid non-recovery or reduced returns.
- Seasonality and demand drivers: Utility margins vary with seasonal weather patterns. Weather deviations, customer counts, temperature variance, historical usage, local economic activity, energy efficiency, and distributed generation all influence retail sales after weather normalization.
- Reliability obligations: Utilities must meet explicit or implicit reliability standards regarding outage duration and frequency, with potential incentives or penalties tied to performance.
- Development and construction strategy: The company develops new generation and retrofits plants to meet customer needs or regulatory requirements, typically seeking regulatory approval to ensure capital recovery and returns for utility projects. For generation growth, focus is on key markets and renewables, evaluating investments against risk-adjusted returns and alternative capital uses. The company often secures long-term offtake contracts prior to construction, pursues non-recourse project financing and partnerships to limit parent equity, and uses third-party EPC with internal oversight of safety, budget, and productivity.
- Organizational structure and segments: Operations are managed through four SBUs—US and Utilities (United States, Puerto Rico, El Salvador), South America (Chile, Colombia, Argentina, Brazil), MCAC (Mexico, Central America, Caribbean), and Eurasia (Europe, Asia). Two lines of business: generation (all SBUs) and utilities (primarily US and Utilities), with utilities also able to sell into wholesale markets in some cases.
- Performance measurement: SBU operating performance is tracked using Adjusted PTC, a non-GAAP metric, with contributions shown by SBU for 2022 and reconciliations provided elsewhere in the Form 10-K.
text:
Reliability of Service — Our utility businesses must meet certain reliability standards, such as duration and frequency of outages. Those
standards may be explicit, with defined performance incentives or penalties, or implicit, where the utility must operate to meet customer and/or
regulator expectations.

title: Development and Construction
heading: Development and Construction
start_phrase: We develop and construct new generation facilities.
summary:
- Explains regulatory frameworks for utility tariffs, including formula-based adjustments, treatment of large unregulated customers, and non-bypassable distribution fees.
- Notes that regulated tariffs are designed to recover operating and fixed costs, account for uncollectibles, service quality, and technical/non-technical losses, requiring utilities to manage costs within tariff assumptions.
- Describes seasonality and weather impacts on operating margins and retail sales, alongside effects from economic activity, energy efficiency, distributed generation, and customer counts.
- Outlines reliability obligations, with explicit or implicit standards that can include performance incentives or penalties.
- Details development and construction strategy: building/retrofitting plants for customer needs or regulatory compliance; prioritizing renewable additions in key growth markets; evaluating projects on strategic fit and risk-adjusted returns versus alternative capital uses (including debt repayment).
- Highlights financing approach: securing long-term contracts pre-construction, using non-recourse project debt and partners to limit equity needs, and employing third-party construction with internal oversight on budget, safety, and efficiency.
- Presents segment structure: four SBUs organized by geography—US and Utilities (US, Puerto Rico, El Salvador), South America (Chile, Colombia, Argentina, Brazil), MCAC (Mexico, Central America, Caribbean), and Eurasia (Europe, Asia).
- Defines two business lines: generation (all SBUs) and utilities (only US and Utilities), with utilities generating/purchasing, transmitting, distributing, and selling electricity to end-users and, in some cases, into the wholesale market.
- States that SBU performance is measured using Adjusted PTC (a non-GAAP metric), with 2022 contributions by SBU and reference to the MD&A for definitions and reconciliations.
text:
Development and Construction
We develop and construct new generation facilities. For our utility business, new plants may be built or existing plants retrofitted in
response to customer needs or to comply with regulatory developments. The projects are developed subject to regulatory approval that permits
recovery of our capital cost and a return on our investment. For our generation businesses, our priority for development is in key growth markets,
where we can leverage our global scale and synergies with our existing businesses by adding renewable energy. We make the decision to invest
in new projects by evaluating the strategic fit, project returns and financial profile against a fair risk-adjusted return for the investment and against
alternative uses of capital, including corporate debt repayment.
In some cases, we enter into long-term contracts for output from new facilities prior to commencing construction. To limit required equity
contributions from The AES Corporation, we also seek non-recourse project debt financing and other sources of capital, including partners, when
it is commercially attractive. We typically contract with a third party to manage construction, although our construction management team
supervises the construction work and tracks progress against the project's budget and the required safety, efficiency and productivity standards.

heading: Segments
start_phrase: The segment reporting structure uses the Company's management reporting structure as its foundation to reflect how the Company manages the businesses internally and is mainly organized by geographic regions which provides a socio-political-economic understanding of our business.
summary:
- Regulatory environment and tariffs: Utilities operate under regulated tariff frameworks designed to recover operating and fixed costs, uncollectible amounts, quality of service, and technical/non-technical losses. Some jurisdictions allow automatic or formula-based adjustments. Large-demand customers may be unregulated, can contract directly with utilities or alternative suppliers, and pay non-bypassable distribution fees. Utilities must control costs to tariffed levels to avoid non-recovery or reduced returns.
- Seasonality and demand drivers: Earnings are seasonally affected by weather; margins vary during the year. Weather, customer counts, temperature deviations, and historical usage patterns influence results. Weather-adjusted retail sales are impacted by local economic activity, energy efficiency, distributed generation, and customer growth.
- Reliability obligations: Utilities must meet explicit or implicit reliability standards governing outage frequency and duration, with potential performance incentives or penalties tied to outcomes.
- Development and construction strategy: The company develops/retrofits generation to meet customer needs or regulatory requirements, typically seeking regulatory approval for cost recovery and allowed returns at utilities. Generation growth prioritizes renewables in key markets leveraging scale. Investment decisions weigh strategic fit, risk-adjusted returns, and alternative capital uses. The company often secures long-term offtake contracts before construction, pursues non-recourse project financing and partners to limit parent equity, and uses third-party constructors under internal oversight for safety, budget, and productivity.
- Segment structure and performance metric: Operations are managed through four geographic SBUs—US and Utilities (United States, Puerto Rico, El Salvador), South America (Chile, Colombia, Argentina, Brazil), MCAC (Mexico, Central America, Caribbean), and Eurasia (Europe, Asia)—across two lines of business: generation (all SBUs) and utilities (US and Utilities). Performance is measured using Adjusted PTC (non-GAAP). “Corporate and Other” houses corporate activities and certain investments. References are made to MD&A and financial statement notes for segment details and non-GAAP reconciliations.
- US and Utilities SBU overview: Comprises 47 generation facilities, two US utilities, and four El Salvador utilities, with 13,108 MW of operating installed capacity. Public registrants include IPALCO (AES Indiana’s parent), AES Ohio, and DPL Inc. Asset listings span El Salvador solar/landfill gas (e.g., Bósforo, Cuscatlán, Nejapa), US gas plants (e.g., Southland—Alamitos, Huntington Beach, Redondo Beach), coal (AES Puerto Rico), extensive wind and solar portfolios (including sPower/Highlander, New York Wind, Buffalo Gap I–III), and multiple energy storage projects (e.g., Alamitos Energy Center, Luna, Lancaster). Entries note ownership interests, commercial operation/acquisition years, contract terms, and counterparties (e.g., Southern California Edison, NYISO, LUMA Energy, Apple, Microsoft, utilities/municipalities). References indicate footnotes and non-GAAP notes for further detail.

Segments
The segment reporting structure uses the Company's management reporting structure as its foundation to reflect how the Company
manages the businesses internally and is mainly organized by geographic regions which provides a socio-political-economic understanding of
our business.
We are organized into four market-oriented SBUs: US and Utilities (United States, Puerto Rico and El Salvador); South America (Chile,
Colombia, Argentina and Brazil); MCAC (Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean); and Eurasia (Europe and Asia) — which are led by our
SBU Presidents. We have two lines of business: generation and utilities. Each of our SBUs participates in our first business line, generation, in
which we own and/or operate power plants to generate and sell power to customers, such as utilities, industrial users, and other intermediaries.
Our US and Utilities SBU participates in our second business line, utilities, in which we own and/or operate utilities to generate or purchase,
distribute, transmit and sell electricity to end-user customers in the residential, commercial, industrial and governmental sectors within a defined
service area. In certain circumstances, our utilities also generate and sell electricity on the wholesale market.

title: Business Description
heading: Business Description —
start_phrase: IPALCO is a holding company whose principal subsidiary is AES Indiana.
summary:
- Overview of US and Utilities facilities, with a referenced map of locations.
- Focus on AES Indiana (IPALCO’s principal subsidiary), an integrated electric utility serving Indianapolis and nearby areas under regulatory oversight, with exclusive service rights over ~528 square miles and ~971,000 residents.
- Generation portfolio: four Indiana plants—Petersburg (coal; Unit 1 retired in 2021; Unit 2 planned retirement in 2023; remaining coal units to convert to natural gas by end of 2025), Harding Street (natural gas/fuel oil turbines plus a 20 MW battery for frequency response), Eagle Valley (CCGT natural gas), and Georgetown (natural-gas peaker).
- Renewable and storage strategy: long-term contracts for 300 MW wind and 94 MW solar; development/acquisition of two major solar projects—Petersburg Solar Project (250 MW solar + 180 MWh storage, targeted 2025 completion pending IURC approval) and Hardy Hills Solar Project (195 MW, targeted 2024 completion pending IURC approval).

text:
Business Description — IPALCO is a holding company whose principal subsidiary is AES Indiana. AES Indiana is an integrated utility that
is engaged primarily in generating, transmitting, distributing, and selling electric energy to retail customers in the city of Indianapolis and
neighboring areas within the state of Indiana and is subject to regulatory authority—see Regulatory Framework and Market Structure below. AES
Indiana has an exclusive right to provide electric service to the customers in its service area, covering about 528 square miles with an estimated
population of approximately 971,000 people. AES Indiana owns and operates four generating stations, all within the state of Indiana. AES
Indiana’s largest generating station, Petersburg, is coal-fired. AES Indiana retired 230 MW Petersburg Unit 1 on May 31, 2021 and has plans to
retire 415 MW Petersburg Unit 2 in 2023, which would result in 630 MW of total retired economic capacity at this station. AES Indiana plans to
convert the remaining two coal units at Petersburg to natural gas by the end of 2025 (see Integrated Resource Plan below). The second largest
station, Harding Street, uses natural gas and fuel oil to power combustion turbines. In addition, AES Indiana operates a 20 MW battery-based
energy storage unit at this location, which provides frequency response. The third station, Eagle Valley, is a CCGT natural gas plant. The fourth
station, Georgetown, is a small peaking station that uses natural gas to power combustion turbines. In addition, AES Indiana helps meet its
customers' energy needs with long-term contracts for the purchase of 300 MW of wind-generated electricity and 94 MW of solar-generated
electricity. In July 2021, AES Indiana executed an agreement to acquire a 250 MW solar and 180 MWh energy storage facility (the "Petersburg
Solar Project"). As amended in October 2022 and subject to IURC approval, the Petersburg Solar Project is now expected to be completed in
2025. In December 2021, AES Indiana completed the acquisition of Hardy Hills Solar Energy LLC, including the development of a 195 MW solar
project (the "Hardy Hills Solar Project"). As amended in December 2022 and subject to IURC approval, the Hardy Hills Solar Project is now
expected to be completed in 2024.

title: Key Financial Drivers
heading: Key Financial Drivers —
start_phrase: AES Indiana's financial results are driven primarily by retail demand, weather, and maintenance costs.
summary:
- Scope: Overview of AES Indiana within AES’s US and Utilities businesses, including service territory, generation portfolio, regulatory environment, financial drivers, capital plans, and resource planning.
- Business description: IPALCO’s principal subsidiary AES Indiana is an integrated electric utility serving Indianapolis and nearby areas (exclusive service right over ~528 square miles; ~971,000 population). Owns four Indiana generating stations: Petersburg (coal; Unit 1—230 MW—retired May 31, 2021; Unit 2—415 MW—planned retirement in 2023; remaining coal units to be converted to natural gas by end of 2025), Harding Street (natural gas/fuel oil CTs plus 20 MW battery for frequency response), Eagle Valley (CCGT natural gas), and Georgetown (small gas peaker).
- Renewables and storage: Long-term contracts for 300 MW wind and 94 MW solar. Petersburg Solar Project (250 MW solar + 180 MWh storage), expected 2025 completion subject to IURC approval. Hardy Hills Solar Energy LLC (195 MW solar), expected 2024 completion subject to IURC approval.
- Key financial drivers: Retail demand, weather, maintenance costs, regulatory outcomes, legislative/regulatory changes, and timely recovery of capital expenditures.
- Regulatory framework and rates: Comprehensive IURC regulation over services, facilities, retail rates, securities, etc. Tariff structure includes base rates and multiple riders: fuel and purchased power (Fuel Adjustment Charge), environmental compliance (with return), RTO cost recovery, sharing of wholesale and capacity margins vs. benchmarks, TDSIC investments (return on/return of), and DSM energy efficiency cost/lost margin/performance incentives. Riders are reviewed periodically; overall rates reviewed with base rate cases.
- Recent base rate order: 2018 IURC order increased annual revenues by $44 million (3%), enabling recovery for the Eagle Valley CCGT and other projects; provided ~$50 million of customer benefits over two years.
- Market operations: Member of MISO; AES Indiana’s assets are dispatched by MISO; participates in day-ahead and real-time markets.
- Development strategy: Capital spending for prudent operations, environmental compliance, and discretionary upgrades to replace aging assets and improve performance.
- TDSIC mechanism: Indiana statute enabling recovery outside base rates for eligible T&D and storage projects via a 5–7 year plan; 80% recovered through periodic adjustments (including return, AFUDC, carrying charges, O&M, depreciation, property taxes), 20% deferred to next base rate case; annual increase capped at 2% of total retail revenues. IURC approved AES Indiana’s seven-year, $1.2 billion TDSIC plan (2020–2026). Annual filings since June 2020; as of Dec 31, 2022, $324 million of equipment approved for TDSIC recovery.
- Integrated Resource Plan (Dec 2022): Presents a Preferred Resource Portfolio characterized as the reasonable least-cost approach that delivers a cleaner, more diverse generation mix to meet retail capacity needs over the coming years.
text:
Key Financial Drivers — AES Indiana's financial results are driven primarily by retail demand, weather, and maintenance costs. In addition,
AES Indiana's financial results are likely to be driven by many other factors including, but not limited to:
•regulatory outcomes and impacts;16 | 2022 Annual Report

title: Regulatory Framework and Market Structure
heading: Regulatory Framework and Market Structure —
start_phrase: AES Indiana is subject to comprehensive regulation by the IURC with respect to its services and facilities, retail rates and charges, the issuance of long-term securities, and certain other matters.

- Highlights regulatory risks tied to new legislation, regulatory changes, and timely recovery of capital expenditures.

- Outlines market participation: AES Indiana is a transmission owner in MISO; MISO dispatches generation and operates day-ahead and real-time markets in which AES Indiana offers electricity.

- Details Indiana’s TDSIC statute enabling recovery for eligible transmission, distribution, and storage projects via a periodic mechanism: 5–7 year plans; 80% of costs (including return, AFUDC, post-in-service carrying charges, O&M, depreciation, property taxes) recovered through riders; 20% deferred to next base rate case; capped at 2% of total retail revenues annually.

text:
Regulatory Framework and Market Structure — AES Indiana is subject to comprehensive regulation by the IURC with respect to its
services and facilities, retail rates and charges, the issuance of long-term securities, and certain other matters. The regulatory authority of the
IURC over AES Indiana's business is typical of regulation generally imposed by state public utility commissions. The IURC sets tariff rates for
electric service provided by AES Indiana. The IURC considers all allowable costs for ratemaking purposes, including a fair return on assets used
and useful to providing service to customers.
AES Indiana's tariff rates for electric service to retail customers consist of basic rates and approved charges. In addition, AES Indiana's
rates include various adjustment mechanisms, including, but not limited to: (i) a rider to reflect changes in fuel and purchased power costs to
meet AES Indiana's retail load requirements, referred to as the Fuel Adjustment Charge, (ii) a rider for the timely recovery of costs incurred to
comply with environmental laws and regulations, including a return, (iii) a rider to reflect changes in ongoing RTO costs, (iv) riders for passing
through to customers wholesale sales margins and capacity sales above and below established annual benchmarks, (v) a rider for a return on,
and of, investments for eligible TDSIC improvements, and (vi) a rider for cost recovery, lost margin recoveries and performance incentives from
AES Indiana's demand side management energy efficiency programs. Each of these tariff rate components function somewhat independently of
one another, but the overall structure of AES Indiana's rates is subject to review at the time of any review of AES Indiana's basic rates and
charges. Additionally, AES Indiana's rider recoveries are reviewed through recurring filings.
On October 31, 2018, the IURC issued an order approving an uncontested settlement agreement to increase AES Indiana's annual
revenues by $44 million, or 3% (the "2018 Base Rate Order"). This revenue increase primarily includes recovery through rates of costs
associated with the CCGT at Eagle Valley, completed in the first half of 2018, and other construction projects. New base rates and charges
became effective on December 5, 2018. The 2018 Base Rate Order was AES Indiana's most recent base rate order and also provided
customers with approximately $50 million in benefits through a rate adjustment mechanism over a two-year period.
AES Indiana is one of many transmission system owner members in MISO, an RTO which maintains functional control over the combined
transmission systems of its members and manages one of the largest energy and ancillary services markets in the U.S. MISO dispatches
generation assets in economic order considering transmission constraints and other reliability issues to meet the total demand in the MISO
region. AES Indiana offers electricity in the MISO day-ahead and real-time markets.

title: Development Strategy
heading: Development Strategy —
start_phrase: AES Indiana's construction program is composed of capital expenditures necessary for prudent utility operations and compliance with environmental regulations, along with discretionary investments designed to replace aging equipment or improve overall performance.
summary:
- Regulatory context: AES Indiana operates under comprehensive IURC oversight covering services, facilities, retail rates, long‑term securities, and related matters. Rates comprise base tariffs plus multiple riders, with recurring reviews and overall structure examined during base rate cases.
- Rate mechanisms: Riders address fuel and purchased power costs (Fuel Adjustment Charge), environmental compliance recovery (with return), RTO cost changes, sharing of wholesale and capacity margins vs. benchmarks, TDSIC investments (return on and of), and demand-side management cost recovery, lost margins, and incentives.
- 2018 base rate order: IURC approved a $44 million (3%) annual revenue increase, largely for the Eagle Valley CCGT and other projects, effective December 5, 2018, and provided about $50 million of customer benefits over two years via a rate adjustment.
- Market participation: AES Indiana is a transmission owner in MISO, which dispatches generation regionally; the company sells into MISO’s day‑ahead and real‑time markets.
- Capital strategy: Focus on necessary and discretionary investments for reliability, environmental compliance, asset replacement, and performance improvement.
- TDSIC framework: Indiana statute enables recovery of eligible transmission, distribution, and storage investments outside base cases via a periodic adjustment—80% recovered contemporaneously (including return, AFUDC, post‑in‑service carrying charges, O&M, depreciation, and property taxes), 20% deferred to next base rate case; capped at 2% of total retail revenues annually; plans must span 5–7 years.
- TDSIC approvals: IURC approved a seven‑year, $1.2 billion plan (2020–2026). AES Indiana files annual TDSIC rate adjustments and staggered plan updates; $324 million of equipment had been approved for TDSIC recovery as of December 31, 2022.
- Integrated Resource Plan (2022): Filed an IRP identifying a preferred, reasonable least‑cost portfolio to meet capacity needs, aiming for a cleaner, more diverse generation mix for customers.
text:
Development Strategy — AES Indiana's construction program is composed of capital expenditures necessary for prudent utility operations
and compliance with environmental regulations, along with discretionary investments designed to replace aging equipment or improve overall
performance.
Senate Enrolled Act 560, the Transmission, Distribution, and Storage System Improvement Charge ("TDSIC") statute, provides for cost
recovery outside of a base rate proceeding for new or replacement electric and gas transmission, distribution, and storage projects that a public
utility undertakes for the purposes of safety, reliability, system modernization, or economic development. Provisions of the TDSIC statute require
that requests for recovery include a plan of at least five years and not more than seven for eligible investments. Once a plan is approved by the
IURC, eighty percent of eligible costs can be recovered using a periodic rate adjustment mechanism, referred to as a TDSIC mechanism.
Recoverable costs include a return on, and of, the investment, including AFUDC, post-in-service carrying charges, operation and maintenance
expenses, depreciation, and property taxes. The remaining twenty percent of recoverable costs are deferred for future recovery in the public
utility’s next base rate case. The TDSIC mechanism is capped at an annual increase of two percent of total retail revenues.
On March 4, 2020, the IURC issued an order approving the projects in AES Indiana's seven-year TDSIC Plan for eligible transmission,
distribution, and storage system improvements totaling $1.2 billion from 2020 through 2026. Beginning in June 2020, AES Indiana files an annual
TDSIC rate adjustment for a return on, and of, investments through March 31 with rates requested to be effective each November. Annual
TDSIC plan update filings are required to be staggered by six months as ordered by the IURC and are filed each December. The total amount of
AES Indiana’s equipment approved for TDSIC recovery as of December 31, 2022 was $324 million.

title: Integrated Resource Plan

- AES Indiana’s participation in MISO’s day-ahead and real-time markets and MISO’s dispatch role.
- Development strategy emphasizing required and discretionary capital investments for reliability, modernization, and environmental compliance.
- Details of Indiana’s TDSIC statute: 5–7 year plans, 80% cost recovery via periodic adjustments (including return and various carrying costs), 20% deferred to next base case, with a 2% annual revenue cap.
- Approval of AES Indiana’s seven-year, $1.2 billion TDSIC plan (2020–2026); annual filings and updates; $324 million of equipment approved for recovery as of December 31, 2022.
- 2022 Integrated Resource Plan: preferred least-cost, cleaner portfolio; plan to convert Petersburg Units 3 and 4 from coal to natural gas by end of 2025 (approvals pending); add up to 1,300 MW of wind, solar, and battery storage by 2027; monitor emerging technologies (green hydrogen, SMRs, carbon capture).
- 2019 IRP actions: retirement of Petersburg Unit 1 (May 31, 2021) and planned retirement of Unit 2 in 2023; IURC approval for creation and recovery of regulatory assets tied to these retirements.
- Renewable and storage projects: acquisition of 195 MW Hardy Hills Solar (operations expected 2024) and 250 MW Petersburg Solar plus 180 MWh storage (operations expected 2025), both IURC-approved.
- Equity funding: $275 million (2021) and $253 million (2022) from AES and CDPQ to support TDSIC and replacement generation projects.
